lesson.title: What Should Have Happened: Calculating Expected Counts
lesson.summary: Expected counts turn the proportions named in a null hypothesis into concrete predicted counts, computed as each hypothesized proportion times the total sample size, and they need not be equal across categories.
lesson.body:
An expected count for a category is the hypothesized population proportion for that category, taken straight from H0, multiplied by the total sample size: expected count equals n times p. This is the step that turns an abstract probability distribution, the kind described in probability distribution, into concrete, checkable numbers you can compare directly against what was actually observed.

An important structural point follows directly from that formula: expected counts do not have to be equal across categories. The die-rolling example earlier happened to have equal expected counts, 10 for every face, only because the null hypothesis itself claimed equal probabilities, 1 divided by 6 for each face. Whenever H0 specifies unequal proportions, the expected counts should be unequal too, in exactly those same proportions.

Continuing the candy example from GOF hypotheses: H0 claims 30 percent red, 25 percent blue, 25 percent yellow, and 20 percent green. A student buys a large sample of n equals 200 candies. The expected counts are: red, 200 times 0.30 equals 60; blue, 200 times 0.25 equals 50; yellow, 200 times 0.25 equals 50; green, 200 times 0.20 equals 40. As a check, these should sum back to the total sample size: 60 plus 50 plus 50 plus 40 equals 200, which matches. Now suppose the actual observed counts turn out to be red 70, blue 45, yellow 55, green 30 (also summing to 200). The chi-square statistic is (70 minus 60) squared over 60, plus (45 minus 50) squared over 50, plus (55 minus 50) squared over 50, plus (30 minus 40) squared over 40, which is 100 divided by 60, plus 25 divided by 50, plus 25 divided by 50, plus 100 divided by 40, or about 1.667 plus 0.5 plus 0.5 plus 2.5, totaling about 5.167. With 4 categories, degrees of freedom is 4 minus 1 equals 3, and the critical value at a significance level of 0.05 with df equals 3 is 7.815. Since 5.167 is less than 7.815, we fail to reject H0. There is not enough evidence that the company's claimed color distribution is incorrect.

One practical habit ties directly back to the conditions in goodness-of-fit test: always compute every expected count before running the test, and check that each one is at least 5. In this example the smallest expected count, 40, comfortably clears that bar. If any expected count had come out below 5, which can happen with small total samples or with categories that are hypothesized to be rare, the chi-square approximation would no longer be reliable and the test should not be used as-is without some adjustment, such as combining categories.
